podcast.title: Meeting of Minds at Spike Island (1990)
podcast.body: Rave culture, which was popular in the late 1980s, converged significantly with the Madchester scene at The Stone Roses' Spike Island concert in May 1990. Attendees from both subcultures discovered commonalities, with "a little ecstasy" facilitating their interaction. "The mad Chester kids and the rave kids went face to face and with the help of a little ecstasy found that they had a lot in common."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1991 Peak and Smiley Irony
podcast.body: Rave culture reached its peak in 1991. However, the smiley face, its iconic symbol, received an ironic response from other artists in the underground scene. "La cultura rift hubo su apojeo en 1991, sin embargo, la corita sonriente tuvo una respuesta ironica a manos de otros abandonados del underground."

podcast.title: Daft Punk's Impact
podcast.body: Daft Punk's Homework was noted as the only album from 90s rave culture that managed to transcend its niche origins and achieve mass consumption.

srcs.episode: Daft Punk: Como el Homework revolucionó la electrónica

podcast.title: Decline of Rave Culture
podcast.body: The club and rave culture that was prominent in the UK during the 1980s had waned by the early 1990s, contributing to a void in homegrown British music. "The club and rave culture that had swept the nation in the 1980s had waned."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Niche Audience in 90s Europe
podcast.body: In the 1990s, pure techno evolved into "Rave Maspura" (rave culture), which catered to a very specific and minority audience predominantly concentrated in Europe. Daft Punk's Homework was initially thought to be a record for professional rave culture.
